decks.title: Thermochemistry — Part 1: Heats of reaction, calorific value and neutralisation
goals: Define the standard enthalpies of formation, combustion, solution, dilution and neutralisation and write thermochemical equations
Calculate the calorific value of a fuel and use a simple calorimeter to find an enthalpy change
Explain why the heat of neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base is constant and why it is lower for weak acids and bases

slides.heading: Heat changes that we can measure and tabulate
slides.body_md: Part 1: the **heats of reaction** — formation, combustion, solution, dilution and neutralisation — and how a calorimeter and the **calorific value** turn them into numbers.

visual.alt: Flow chart of the topics of Part 1

slides.narration: Welcome to Part One of thermochemistry. Every chemical change takes in or gives out heat, and the heat of reaction is the enthalpy change measured at constant pressure. We meet the special names for these heats: formation, combustion, solution, dilution and neutralisation, and then measure them with a calorimeter.

slides.heading: The enthalpy change of a reaction
slides.body_md: The **enthalpy of reaction** ΔH is the heat exchanged at constant pressure when the reaction occurs in the **molar amounts shown by the equation**. **ΔH < 0**: exothermic, heat given out. **ΔH > 0**: endothermic. A **thermochemical equation** states the physical states and the value of ΔH. **Standard** values refer to 1 bar and the stated temperature (298 K).

rows: solute dissolved in a large amount of solvent
solution made more dilute with solvent
water formed from acid and base

visual.alt: Table of the types of heat of reaction with examples

slides.narration: The enthalpy of reaction is the heat exchanged at constant pressure for the amounts shown in the equation. A negative value means heat is given out, and a positive value means heat is taken in. A thermochemical equation states the physical states and the value, and standard values refer to one bar pressure and two hundred ninety eight kelvin.

slides.heading: Standard enthalpy of formation and of combustion
slides.body_md:
**Formation, ΔfH°:** one mole of a compound is formed from its **elements in their standard states**; by convention ΔfH° of an element in its standard state is **zero**. Example: $\ce{2C(graphite) + 3H2(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> C2H5OH(l)}$, −277.7 kJ mol⁻¹.

**Combustion, ΔcH°:** one mole of a substance **burns completely in excess oxygen**; always **negative**. Example: $\ce{CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)}$, −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of standard enthalpies of formation used in this chapter

slides.narration: The standard enthalpy of formation is the heat change when one mole of a compound is made from its elements in their standard states. For an element in its standard state it is zero by convention. The enthalpy of combustion is the heat change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen, and it is always negative.

slides.heading: Formation and combustion are linked
slides.body_md: For methane: **ΔfH(CH₄) + ΔcH(CH₄) = ΔfH(CO₂) + 2ΔfH(H₂O)**, so $\Delta_cH = [-393.5 + 2(-285.8)] - (-74.8) = -890.3$ kJ mol⁻¹. The energy-level diagram shows both routes from the elements to the products.

slides.narration: Write the balanced combustion equation. Add up the formation enthalpies of the products, three carbon dioxide and four liquid water, and subtract the formation enthalpy of propane. slides.heading: Enthalpy of solution and of dilution
slides.body_md: The **enthalpy of solution** is the enthalpy change when **one mole of solute dissolves** in a specified, large amount of solvent. It is the balance of the energy to separate the particles (**absorbed**) and the energy of **hydration** (**released**): exothermic for NaOH, endothermic for NH₄NO₃. The **enthalpy of dilution** is the heat change when more solvent is added to a solution.

visual.alt: Table of enthalpies of solution and their effect on the temperature

slides.narration: The enthalpy of solution is the heat change when one mole of solute dissolves in a large amount of solvent. It balances the energy needed to separate the particles against the energy released when they are hydrated. Sodium hydroxide warms the water, while ammonium nitrate cools it. Dilution of a solution also changes the heat content.

slides.heading: Measuring a heat change: the calorimeter
slides.body_md: In a **solution calorimeter** (insulated cup, lid, thermometer, stirrer) the heat absorbed by the solution is **q = m c ΔT**, with c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and density 1 g cm⁻³. The heat of reaction is the same size and opposite in sign: **ΔH = −q / n**, where n is the number of moles of the limiting reagent.

slides.narration: A simple calorimeter is an insulated cup with a lid, a thermometer and a stirrer. The heat taken up by the solution is the mass times the specific heat times the temperature rise. The enthalpy change of the reaction has the opposite sign, and it is divided by the number of moles of the limiting reagent to give the value per mole.

slides.heading: Calorific value of a fuel
slides.body_md: The **calorific value** is the heat released when **unit mass** of a fuel burns completely, in **kJ g⁻¹** (or kJ kg⁻¹). **Calorific value = −ΔcH / M.** Hydrogen has the highest value among common fuels, so rockets use it.

slides.narration: The calorific value of a fuel is the heat released when one gram burns completely. It equals minus the enthalpy of combustion divided by the molar mass. Hydrogen is far ahead of the other fuels, with about one hundred forty three kilojoules per gram. The hydrocarbons are close to fifty, while ethanol and glucose give much less.

slides.heading: Worked example: a propane cylinder
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A cylinder holds 14.2 kg of propane (M = 44 g mol⁻¹, ΔcH = -2219.9 kJ mol⁻¹). Find the calorific value and the heat from one cylinder.

Calorific value $= \dfrac{2219.9}{44} = 50.50$ kJ g⁻¹ (taking 50.5 kJ g⁻¹).

Heat $= 14\,200 \times 50.45 \approx 7.16 \times 10^{5}$ kJ.

visual.alt: Table of the calorific value and heat from a propane cylinder

slides.narration: Divide the enthalpy of combustion by the molar mass to get the heat per gram, about fifty point five kilojoules. The cylinder holds fourteen thousand two hundred grams of propane, so multiply, and the heat is about seven hundred sixteen thousand kilojoules. Check by finding the moles of propane and multiplying by the heat per mole.

slides.body_md: Convert the mass to moles, then multiply by the heat per mole.
slides.narration: Quick check. Divide the mass of the propane by its molar mass to find the moles. Then multiply by the magnitude of the enthalpy of combustion. Remember that the heat released is a positive quantity in this question, which asks for the heat given out.

slides.heading: Heat of neutralisation of strong acids and bases
slides.body_md: The **enthalpy of neutralisation** is the heat released when an acid and a base react to form **one mole of water**. For any **strong acid + strong base** in dilute solution it is nearly constant, **−57.1 kJ mol⁻¹**: both are completely ionised, so the spectator ions do not change and the net reaction is always $\ce{H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l)}$. For H₂SO₄ the value is quoted per mole of water (−114.2 kJ per mole of acid).

slides.narration: When a strong acid reacts with a strong base in dilute solution, both are completely ionised. The other ions are only spectators, so the net change is hydrogen ions combining with hydroxide ions to form water. That is why every such pair gives the same heat, about fifty seven kilojoules per mole of water.

slides.heading: Why weak acids and bases give less heat
slides.body_md: A **weak acid** is only partly ionised. As the base removes H⁺, more molecules must ionise, and **ionisation absorbs energy**. So the heat released is **less** than 57.1 kJ mol⁻¹; the shortfall is roughly the **enthalpy of ionisation**. The weaker the acid, the larger the shortfall.

visual.alt: Table of the heat of neutralisation and the energy of ionisation of weak acids

slides.narration: A weak acid is only partly ionised. During neutralisation more molecules have to ionise, and ionisation absorbs energy. This reduces the heat released. The weaker the acid, the larger the shortfall from fifty seven kilojoules. Ethanoic acid falls short by about two, while hydrogen cyanide falls short by about forty five.

slides.heading: Worked example: temperature rise on neutralisation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 50 cm³ of 2.0 M HCl is mixed with 50 cm³ of 2.0 M NaOH. Find the temperature rise (ΔH = −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹; c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; density 1 g cm⁻³).

Moles of water $= 0.050 \times 2.0 = 0.10$ mol. $q = 0.10 \times 57\,100 = 5710$ J. Mass $= 100$ g.

$\Delta T = \dfrac{q}{mc} = \dfrac{5710}{100 \times 4.18} = 13.7$ K.

visual.alt: Table of the temperature-rise calculation for an acid-base mixture

slides.narration: First find the moles of water formed from the volume and the molarity. Multiply by the molar heat of neutralisation to get the heat in joules. Then divide by the mass of the solution times its specific heat. The temperature rises by about thirteen point seven kelvin for these concentrated solutions.

slides.heading: Quick check: the limiting reagent
slides.body_md: Compare the moles of H⁺ and OH⁻; the smaller one fixes the water formed.
slides.narration: Quick check. Work out the moles of hydrogen ions from the acid and the moles of hydroxide ions from the base. The reagent present in the smaller amount limits how much water forms. Use that amount to find the heat, and then the total mass of solution.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: ΔfH°: one mole of compound from its elements in standard states (zero for an element); ΔcH°: one mole burnt completely, always negative.
ΔcH = Σ ΔfH(products) − Σ ΔfH(reactants); the enthalpies of solution and dilution depend on hydration against separation of the particles.
Calorimeter: q = m c ΔT; ΔH = −q / n. Calorific value = −ΔcH / M in kJ g⁻¹.
Strong acid + strong base: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, ΔH = −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹ of water.
Weak acids and bases release less because ionisation absorbs energy (CH₃COOH −55.2, HCN −12.1 kJ mol⁻¹).

visual.alt: Summary table of the key ideas of Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part One. Formation and combustion enthalpies are linked, and combustion is always negative. A calorimeter gives the heat from the temperature rise. Calorific value is the heat per gram of fuel. Strong acids and bases always release about fifty seven kilojoules per mole of water, and weak ones release less because ionisation takes in energy.

slides.heading: Enthalpies of breaking and changing
slides.body_md: Part 2: enthalpies of **bond dissociation, atomisation, sublimation, phase change and ionisation**, then **Hess’s law**, which lets us add them up.

visual.alt: Table of the enthalpies of Part 2

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two. Here we meet the enthalpies that tell us how much energy it takes to break bonds, to make atoms, to change a solid into a vapour and to remove electrons. All of them are positive. Then Hess law shows how to add enthalpy changes to find values that cannot be measured directly.

slides.heading: Bond dissociation and mean bond enthalpy
slides.body_md: The **bond dissociation enthalpy** is the energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond in a **gaseous** molecule. In a polyatomic molecule the values for one kind of bond differ a little, so a **mean bond enthalpy** is tabulated. **ΔH(reaction) = Σ (bonds broken) − Σ (bonds formed)**: breaking costs energy, forming releases it.

visual.alt: Table of mean bond enthalpies

slides.narration: The bond dissociation enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of a bond in a gaseous molecule. Because the value differs slightly between molecules, tables give mean values. The enthalpy of a reaction is the sum of the energies of the bonds broken minus the sum of the energies of the bonds formed.

slides.heading: Enthalpy of atomisation
slides.body_md: The **enthalpy of atomisation** is the enthalpy change when **one mole of gaseous atoms** is formed from the element (or compound) in its standard state. For a metal it equals the **enthalpy of sublimation**; for a diatomic gas it is **half the bond dissociation enthalpy**: $\ce{1/2Cl2(g) -> Cl(g)}$, 121 kJ mol⁻¹. For a compound, such as $\ce{CH4(g) -> C(g) + 4H(g)}$, it is the sum of the bond enthalpies broken.

visual.alt: Table of enthalpies of atomisation of some elements

slides.narration: The enthalpy of atomisation is the heat needed to form one mole of gaseous atoms. For a solid element such as carbon or sodium it equals the enthalpy of sublimation. For a diatomic gas such as chlorine it is half of the bond dissociation enthalpy, because one mole of molecules gives two moles of atoms.

slides.heading: Worked example: ΔH from bond enthalpies
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Estimate ΔH for $\ce{HC#CH(g) + HCl(g) -> H2C=CHCl(g)}$ (C≡C 837, H–Cl 431, C=C 611, C–H 414, C–Cl 326 kJ mol⁻¹).

Broken: C≡C + H–Cl $= 837 + 431 = 1268$ kJ. Formed: C=C + C–H + C–Cl $= 611 + 414 + 326 = 1351$ kJ.

$\Delta H = 1268 - 1351 = -83$ kJ mol⁻¹: exothermic.

slides.narration: List the bonds broken: one carbon carbon triple bond and one hydrogen chlorine bond, which cost one thousand two hundred sixty eight kilojoules. List the bonds formed: a double bond, a carbon hydrogen bond and a carbon chlorine bond, which release one thousand three hundred fifty one. The difference is minus eighty three, so the reaction is exothermic.

slides.heading: Ionisation enthalpy
slides.body_md: The **ionisation enthalpy** is the energy needed to remove an electron from a **gaseous** atom or ion: $\ce{Na(g) -> Na+(g) + e-}$, +496 kJ mol⁻¹. It is **always positive**, and each successive electron costs more: Mg 738 then 1451 kJ mol⁻¹. To reach a gaseous ion from the **solid metal** we add the sublimation enthalpy first.

visual.alt: Table of sublimation and ionisation enthalpies of sodium and magnesium

slides.narration: The ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom. It is always positive, and the second electron costs more than the first because it is removed from a positive ion. For a solid metal we first sublime the metal to gaseous atoms, and then add the ionisation enthalpy.

slides.heading: Worked example: potassium solid to gaseous ions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find ΔH for $\ce{K(s) -> K+(g) + e-}$ given ΔsubH(K) = 89.0 and the ionisation enthalpy of K = 419 kJ mol⁻¹.

Step 1: $\ce{K(s) -> K(g)}$, +89.0. Step 2: $\ce{K(g) -> K+(g) + e-}$, +419.

$\Delta H = 89.0 + 419 = 508.0$ kJ mol⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the sublimation and ionisation steps for potassium

slides.narration: Break the change into two steps. First the solid potassium becomes gaseous atoms, which takes eighty nine kilojoules. Then each gaseous atom loses an electron, which takes four hundred nineteen kilojoules. Add the two steps, and the total is five hundred eight kilojoules for each mole of potassium.

slides.heading: Hess’s law of constant heat summation
slides.body_md: The **total enthalpy change** of a reaction is the **same whether it takes place in one step or several**, because **H is a state function**. Here **ΔH₃ = ΔH₁ + ΔH₂**: N₂ + 2O₂ → 2NO₂ directly (+66.4 kJ) or via 2NO (+180.6, then −114.2).

slides.narration: Hess law states that the total enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whether it happens in one step or in several steps. This is because enthalpy is a state function. In the diagram, going directly from nitrogen and oxygen to nitrogen dioxide gives the same change as going by way of nitric oxide, so the two steps add up to the direct value.

slides.heading: Using Hess’s law
slides.body_md: **1.** Add equations (reverse an equation: change the sign of ΔH; multiply an equation: multiply ΔH). **2.** From **formation data**, ΔH = Σ ΔfH(products) − Σ ΔfH(reactants). **3.** From **combustion data**, ΔH = Σ ΔcH(reactants) − Σ ΔcH(products). **4.** From **bond enthalpies:** broken − formed.

visual.alt: Table of the ways of using Hess law

slides.narration: There are four ways to use Hess law. Add the given equations, reversing one changes the sign of the enthalpy change, and multiplying one multiplies it. With formation data, subtract the reactant sum from the product sum. With combustion data, do the opposite. With bond enthalpies, subtract the bonds formed from the bonds broken.

slides.heading: Worked example: formation of ethene from combustion data
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find ΔfH of ethene from ΔcH: C(graphite) −393.5, H₂ −285.8, C₂H₄ −1410.9 kJ mol⁻¹ (given).

Target: $\ce{2C(graphite) + 2H2(g) -> C2H4(g)}$.

$\Delta_fH = 2(-393.5) + 2(-285.8) - (-1410.9) = -787.0 - 571.6 + 1410.9 = +52.3$ kJ mol⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the Hess calculation of the enthalpy of formation of ethene

slides.narration: The target is two carbon and two hydrogen forming ethene. Burn the carbon, which gives minus seven hundred eighty seven. Burn the hydrogen, which gives minus five hundred seventy one point six. Then reverse the combustion of ethene, which gives plus fourteen hundred ten point nine. The sum is plus fifty two point three kilojoules.

slides.heading: Quick check: an enthalpy cycle for hydration
slides.body_md: Both the anhydrous salt and its hydrate lead to the same solution.
slides.narration: Quick check. Draw a cycle in which both the anhydrous salt with water and the hydrate dissolve to give the same solution. The hydration step plus the solution of the hydrate equals the solution of the anhydrous salt. Rearrange this to find the hydration enthalpy, and watch the signs.

slides.heading: Worked example: dehydrogenation of ethane
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find ΔH for $\ce{C2H6(g) -> C2H4(g) + H2(g)}$ from ΔfH (C₂H₆ −84.7, C₂H₄ +52.3 kJ mol⁻¹).

$\Delta H = [\Delta_fH(\ce{C2H4}) + \Delta_fH(\ce{H2})] - \Delta_fH(\ce{C2H6}) = [+52.3 + 0] - (-84.7) = +137.0$ kJ mol⁻¹: endothermic.

visual.alt: Table of the dehydrogenation of ethane from enthalpies of formation

slides.narration: Use the formation enthalpies. The products are ethene, with plus fifty two point three, and hydrogen, which is an element and has zero. The reactant is ethane with minus eighty four point seven. Product sum minus reactant sum gives plus one hundred thirty seven kilojoules, so the reaction is endothermic and needs heating.

slides.heading: Quick check: formation of nitrogen dioxide
slides.body_md: Add the two equations first; then divide by the number of moles of NO₂.
slides.narration: Quick check. Add the two given equations so that the nitric oxide cancels. This gives the enthalpy change for forming two moles of nitrogen dioxide from the elements. The enthalpy of formation is defined per mole, so divide the total by two before giving your answer.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Bond dissociation, atomisation, sublimation, fusion, vaporisation and ionisation enthalpies are all positive; ΔatomH of a diatomic gas is half its bond enthalpy.
ΔH(reaction) from bond enthalpies = Σ broken − Σ formed (an estimate, as mean values are used).
ΔsubH = ΔfusH + ΔvapH at one temperature; ionisation enthalpies rise with each electron removed.
Hess’s law: ΔH is the same by any route because H is a state function.
Reverse an equation: change sign of ΔH; multiply an equation: multiply ΔH.

visual.alt: Summary table of the methods of Part 2

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part Two. The enthalpies of bond dissociation, atomisation, sublimation, phase change and ionisation are all positive. Bond enthalpies give an estimate of a reaction enthalpy, bonds broken minus bonds formed. Hess law lets us add or subtract steps, and the same total results by any route, because enthalpy is a state function.

notes.title: Thermochemistry — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Enthalpy of reaction: formation and combustion
sections.body_md:
The **enthalpy of reaction** ΔH is the heat exchanged at constant pressure for the molar amounts in the balanced equation (ΔH < 0 exothermic, ΔH > 0 endothermic). A **thermochemical equation** shows physical states and ΔH; **standard** values refer to 1 bar (and 298 K).

**Standard enthalpy of formation, ΔfH°:** one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states; it is **zero** for an element in its standard state (graphite for carbon, so diamond is +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹). Example: $\ce{C(graphite) + O2(g) -> CO2(g)}$, −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

**Standard enthalpy of combustion, ΔcH°:** one mole of a substance burns completely in excess oxygen; always **negative**. The combustion of hydrogen to liquid water and of graphite to CO₂ are also formation reactions. From formation data, $\Delta_cH = \sum \Delta_fH(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_fH(\text{reactants})$; for methane, −393.5 + 2(−285.8) − (−74.8) = −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹.

key_terms.definition_md: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states.
The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in excess oxygen; always negative.
The most stable form of a substance at 1 bar and the stated temperature, usually 298 K.
A balanced equation with physical states and the enthalpy change.

sections.heading: 2. Enthalpy of solution and dilution; calorimetry
sections.body_md:
The **enthalpy of solution** is the enthalpy change when one mole of solute dissolves in a large amount of solvent: it balances the energy to separate the particles (absorbed) against hydration (released). NaOH(s) −44.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (warms), NH₄NO₃(s) +25.7 (cools), CuSO₄(s) −66.5, CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) +11.7. The **enthalpy of dilution** is the heat change when more solvent is added to a solution (negative for concentrated H₂SO₄).

In a **solution calorimeter** the heat absorbed is $q = mc\Delta T$ ($c = 4.18$ J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; density 1 g cm⁻³) and $\Delta H = -q/n$, with n the moles of the limiting reagent.

key_terms.definition_md: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance dissolves in a specified large amount of solvent.
The heat change when a solution is diluted by adding more solvent at constant pressure.
An insulated vessel with a thermometer in which the temperature change of a reaction is measured.

sections.heading: 3. Calorific value of a fuel
sections.body_md: The **calorific value** of a fuel is the heat released when unit mass burns completely, in kJ g⁻¹ or kJ kg⁻¹: **calorific value = −ΔcH / M**. Hydrogen 142.9; methane 55.6; propane 50.5 (so 14.2 kg gives about 7.16 × 10⁵ kJ); ethyne 50.0; ethanol 29.7; glucose 15.6 kJ g⁻¹. A good fuel has a high calorific value, burns cleanly and is easy to store and transport.

key_terms.definition_md: The heat produced by the complete combustion of unit mass of a fuel, in kJ g⁻¹.

sections.heading: 4. Heat of neutralisation
sections.body_md:
The **enthalpy of neutralisation** is the heat released when an acid and a base react to form **one mole of water**. For a **strong acid with a strong base** in dilute solution it is nearly constant, **−57.1 kJ mol⁻¹**, because both are completely ionised and the spectator ions do not change: $\ce{H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l)}$. For H₂SO₄ and NaOH the value is −57.1 per mole of water (−114.2 per mole of acid).

With a **weak acid or base** less heat is released, because ionisation absorbs energy: CH₃COOH −55.2 (shortfall 1.9), HCN −12.1 (shortfall 45.0 kJ mol⁻¹).

key_terms.definition_md: The heat released when an acid and a base react to form one mole of water.
Ions present in the solution that do not change during the reaction.
The enthalpy change when one mole of a weak electrolyte ionises completely in solution.

sections.heading: 5. Bond, atomisation, sublimation, phase-transition and ionisation enthalpies
sections.body_md:
**Bond dissociation enthalpy:** energy to break one mole of a bond in a gaseous molecule (mean values in tables: H–H 436, C–H 414, C–C 347, C=C 611, C≡C 837, O=O 498, Cl–Cl 242 kJ mol⁻¹). **ΔH(reaction) ≈ Σ broken − Σ formed**, an estimate for gases.

**Atomisation:** one mole of gaseous atoms from the element or compound (C 716.7; ½Cl₂ → Cl 121). **Sublimation:** solid → vapour. **Fusion and vaporisation** (water 6.01 and 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹): the temperature stays constant during the change; ΔsubH = ΔfusH + ΔvapH. **Ionisation enthalpy:** X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻, always positive (Na 496; Mg 738 then 1451 kJ mol⁻¹).

key_terms.definition_md: The energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond in a gaseous molecule.
The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element or compound.
The enthalpy change when one mole of a solid changes directly into vapour.
The energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms or ions.

sections.heading: 6. Hess’s law and its applications
sections.body_md:
**Hess’s law:** the total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it takes place in one step or in several steps, because enthalpy is a **state function**. Add equations to reach the target; **reversing** an equation changes the sign of ΔH; **multiplying** it multiplies ΔH.

**Uses:** ΔfH of a compound from enthalpies of combustion (ethene +52.3 from −393.5, −285.8 and −1410.9); ΔH of a reaction from ΔfH (ΣΔfH products − Σ reactants) or from ΔcH (Σ reactants − Σ products); enthalpies of hydration from solution enthalpies (CuSO₄: −78.2 kJ mol⁻¹); enthalpy of atomisation from a cycle; graphite → diamond +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Quoting ΔfH of an element in its standard state as non-zero, or ΔcH as positive.
- Using bonds formed minus bonds broken, or forgetting to count all the bonds in a molecule.
- Giving calorific value in kJ mol⁻¹ instead of kJ g⁻¹.
- Forgetting to find the limiting reagent before using ΔH = −q / n.
- Explaining the low heat of neutralisation of weak acids without mentioning that ionisation absorbs energy.
- Not changing the sign of ΔH when an equation is reversed in a Hess cycle.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Definitions: the amount (one mole), the state of the substances and the condition (1 bar, 298 K) (1 each).
- Calorimetry: q = m c ΔT (1), moles (1), ΔH per mole with sign and unit (1).
- Hess's law: target equation or cycle (1), correct manipulation with signs (1), numerical answer with unit (1).
- Bond enthalpies: bonds broken (1), bonds formed (1), difference with sign (1).

cards.back_md: Zero, by convention (for example graphite, O₂(g), H₂(g)).

cards.back_md: The energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond in a gaseous molecule.

questions.stem_md: A thermochemistry teacher asks the class to pick the equation whose enthalpy change is the standard enthalpy of formation of liquid ethanol. The correct choice is:
questions.solution_md: The standard enthalpy of formation refers to one mole of the compound formed from its elements in their standard states (graphite, H₂ gas, O₂ gas). Only one option starts from the elements in those states; the others start from compounds or from gaseous atoms — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A rocket engineer burns hydrogen in oxygen and condenses the product to liquid water. The enthalpy change per mole of hydrogen burnt, −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹, is numerically also the standard enthalpy of:
questions.solution_md: $\ce{H2(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> H2O(l)}$ is at once the combustion of one mole of H₂ and the formation of one mole of liquid water from its elements, so the two enthalpies are the same — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A school technician compares three fuels. Methane has ΔcH = −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (M = 16 g mol⁻¹), propane −2219.9 kJ mol⁻¹ (M = 44) and ethanol −1366.7 kJ mol⁻¹ (M = 46). The fuel with the highest calorific value per gram is:

options.text_md: propane, because it has the largest heat of combustion per mole (50.5 kJ g⁻¹ only)
all three are equal, since calorific value does not depend on the molar mass

questions.solution_md: Calorific value = −ΔcH / M. Methane: 890.3 / 16 = 55.6 kJ g⁻¹; propane: 2219.9 / 44 = 50.5; ethanol: 1366.7 / 46 = 29.7. Methane gives the most heat per gram — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Pellets of ammonium nitrate are dissolved in the water of an instant cold pack for sports injuries. The enthalpy of solution of NH₄NO₃ is +25.7 kJ mol⁻¹ (given). As the pellets dissolve, the pack:

options.text_md: warms, because every dissolution releases heat
cools, because the dissolution absorbs heat from the water
stays at the same temperature, because the enthalpy change is small
warms, because the ions are hydrated by the water

questions.solution_md: A positive enthalpy of solution means the dissolution is endothermic: the energy needed to separate the ions exceeds the energy released on hydration, so heat flows in from the water and the pack cools — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The heat change when more solvent is added to a solution, lowering its concentration, at constant pressure, is called the enthalpy of:
questions.solution_md: Adding solvent to an existing solution to make it more dilute is dilution, and the heat change is the enthalpy of dilution. Solution refers to dissolving a solute in a solvent — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A cooking-gas supplier quotes the energy content of its product in kJ per kilogram. This quantity is called the:
questions.solution_md: The calorific value of a fuel is the heat produced by the complete combustion of unit mass of the fuel (kJ g⁻¹ or kJ kg⁻¹) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The enthalpy of combustion of graphite is −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of diamond is −395.4 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement about their standard enthalpies of formation is correct?

options.text_md: graphite is zero by convention, and diamond is +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹
both are zero, since both are forms of carbon
graphite is −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and diamond is −395.4 kJ mol⁻¹
diamond is zero, since it is the harder form

questions.solution_md: The standard state of carbon is graphite, the most stable form, so its ΔfH° is zero. For diamond, ΔfH° = ΔcH(graphite) − ΔcH(diamond) = -393.5 − (-395.4) = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student copying values from a thermochemical data book notices the superscript ° on every enthalpy. The standard state to which these values refer is:

options.text_md: the substance at 273 K and 1 atm, the conditions called STP
the substance cooled to absolute zero
a solution of the substance of concentration 1 M at its boiling point
the pure substance at 1 bar pressure and a stated temperature, usually 298 K

questions.solution_md: Standard enthalpies refer to substances in their standard states: the pure substance (pure solid, pure liquid or ideal gas) at 1 bar, at a temperature that must be stated, usually 298 K. STP (273 K) is a gas-volume convention, not the thermochemical standard state — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The heat log of a cement kiln records the decomposition of limestone, $\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$, with ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹. From the sign of ΔH the kiln engineer concludes that the reaction:

options.text_md: releases heat, so the kiln can run once it is started
takes place with no exchange of heat with the surroundings
absorbs heat, so the kiln must keep supplying energy while it runs
gives products whose total enthalpy is lower than that of the reactants

questions.solution_md: A positive ΔH means the products have more enthalpy than the reactants: the reaction is endothermic and draws heat from the surroundings, so the kiln must be heated throughout — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A trekking team's burner uses 220 g of propane (M = 44 g mol⁻¹, ΔcH = −2219.9 kJ mol⁻¹). Calculate the heat released, in kJ, when all of it burns completely.
Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ (M = 180 g mol⁻¹), is the main fuel of our muscle cells, with ΔcH = −2803 kJ mol⁻¹ (given). Calculate its calorific value in kJ g⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Calorific value $= \dfrac{-\Delta_cH}{M} = \dfrac{2803}{180} = 15.57$ kJ g⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The calorific value of a fuel is normally quoted per mole of the fuel, in kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: False. Calorific value is the heat from burning unit mass of fuel, in kJ g⁻¹ or kJ kg⁻¹; the heat per mole is the enthalpy of combustion.

questions.stem_md: The heat evolved when one mole of a substance burns completely in excess oxygen, with the products in their standard states, is its standard enthalpy of ___.
questions.solution_md: This defines the standard enthalpy of combustion, ΔcH°; it is always negative.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The enthalpy of combustion of hydrogen gas to liquid water is the same number as the enthalpy of formation of liquid water.

**Reason (R):** The standard enthalpy of combustion of every substance is negative.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. But the equality of the two numbers arises because the same equation, H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), serves for both definitions; the sign of ΔcH does not explain it — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The standard enthalpy of formation of graphite is zero but that of diamond is not.

**Reason (R):** By convention, the standard enthalpy of formation of the most stable form of an element in its standard state is taken as zero.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Graphite is the most stable form of carbon under standard conditions, so its ΔfH° is zero by convention; diamond is less stable and its ΔfH° is +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each fuel with its calorific value, calculated from its enthalpy of combustion.
questions.solution_md: Calorific value = −ΔcH / M: hydrogen 285.8/2 = 142.9; propane 2219.9/44 = 50.5; ethanol 1366.7/46 = 29.7; glucose 2803/180 = 15.6 kJ g⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: Define the standard enthalpy of formation and the standard enthalpy of combustion of a substance, and write the thermochemical equation for the formation of liquid water.

answer.model_answer_md: The standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states. The standard enthalpy of combustion is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in excess oxygen, the products being in their standard states. For water: H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔfH° = −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: ΔfH°: 1 mol from elements; ΔcH°: 1 mol burnt completely; H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), −285.8.

questions.stem_md: Define the enthalpy of solution. A student dissolves 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide (M = 40 g mol⁻¹) in water; the enthalpy of solution of NaOH is −44.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (given). Calculate the heat released.

answer.model_answer_md: The enthalpy of solution is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance dissolves in a specified (very large) amount of solvent. Moles of NaOH = 4.0 / 40 = 0.1 mol; heat released = 0.1 × 44.5 = 4.45 kJ.

questions.solution_md: 4.45 kJ released.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the enthalpy of dilution? Why does the solution of a concentrated acid, such as sulfuric acid, become noticeably warm when water is added to it?

answer.model_answer_md: The enthalpy of dilution is the heat change when a solution is diluted by adding more solvent at constant pressure. For a concentrated strong acid the ions (and molecules) are more strongly hydrated in the dilute solution, so the energy released in the extra solvation is large and ΔH is negative; the heat is given out and the solution warms.

questions.solution_md: Heat change on adding solvent; hydration releases energy, ΔH negative.

marking_scheme.step: Extra hydration releases heat: ΔH negative

questions.stem_md: A welder uses ethyne, C₂H₂ (M = 26 g mol⁻¹), for his torch. Using ΔfH values (CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8, C₂H₂ +226.7 kJ mol⁻¹) calculate the enthalpy of combustion of ethyne and its calorific value.
questions.solution_md: $\Delta_cH = -1299.5$ kJ mol⁻¹; calorific value $= 50.0$ kJ g⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: A cooking-gas cylinder holds 14.2 kg of propane (M = 44 g mol⁻¹). Using ΔfH values (C₃H₈ −103.8, CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹), find the enthalpy of combustion of propane, its calorific value, and the heat available from one full cylinder.
questions.solution_md: $\Delta_cH = -2219.9$ kJ mol⁻¹; 50.45 kJ g⁻¹; about $7.16 \times 10^{5}$ kJ.

questions.stem_md: A student dissolves 5.0 g of ammonium nitrate (M = 80 g mol⁻¹) in 100 g of water in an insulated cup. The enthalpy of solution is +25.7 kJ mol⁻¹. Taking the specific heat of the solution as 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and its mass as 105 g, calculate the fall in temperature.

answer.model_answer_md: Moles $= 5.0/80 = 0.0625$ mol. Heat absorbed $= 0.0625 \times 25.7 = 1.606$ kJ $= 1606$ J. From $q = mc\Delta T$: $\Delta T = 1606/(105 \times 4.18) \approx 3.7$ K fall.

questions.solution_md: $\Delta T = 1606/(105 \times 4.18) \approx 3.7$ K.

marking_scheme.step: ΔT = q / (m c) = 3.7 K, a fall

questions.stem_md: A student finds that hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide, and nitric acid with potassium hydroxide, each release almost 57 kJ per mole of water formed. This constancy is because:

options.text_md: every acid contains the same number of ions per mole
the same mass of water is formed in each case
the metal ions react with the acid anions and release equal heat
strong acids and strong bases are completely ionised, so the only net change is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)

questions.solution_md: In dilute solution a strong acid and a strong base are fully ionised, so the spectator ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, NO₃⁻) do not change and the common net reaction is the combination of H⁺ and OH⁻ to form water, with ΔH ≈ −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a dye factory's quality test, 100 cm³ of 1.0 M sulfuric acid is mixed with 200 cm³ of 1.0 M sodium hydroxide. Taking the heat of neutralisation as −57.1 kJ per mole of water, the heat released is about:
questions.solution_md: H⁺ from the acid = 2 × 0.100 = 0.200 mol; OH⁻ = 0.200 mol, so 0.200 mol of water forms. Heat = 0.200 × 57.1 = 11.42 kJ ≈ 11.4 kJ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The heat released when hydrogen cyanide solution is neutralised by sodium hydroxide is only 12.1 kJ per mole of water, against 57.1 kJ for hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide. Taking the difference as the energy spent in ionising the weak acid, the enthalpy of ionisation of HCN is about:
questions.solution_md: The weak acid must ionise as the neutralisation proceeds, absorbing energy. Enthalpy of ionisation ≈ 57.1 − 12.1 = +45.0 kJ mol⁻¹ (endothermic) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a school experiment, 50 cm³ of 1.0 M nitric acid is mixed with 80 cm³ of 0.50 M potassium hydroxide. Assume a heat of neutralisation of −57.1 kJ per mole of water, a solution density of 1 g cm⁻³ and a specific heat of 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. The temperature rise is closest to:
questions.solution_md: Acid = 0.050 mol H⁺, base = 0.040 mol OH⁻, so the base is limiting: 0.040 mol of water forms. q = 0.040 × 57 100 = 2284 J. ΔT = q / (m c) = 2284 / (130 × 4.18) = 4.2 K — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student mixes 75 cm³ of 1.0 M nitric acid with 75 cm³ of 1.0 M potassium hydroxide in an insulated cup and records a temperature rise of 6.7 K (given). Taking the density of the solution as 1 g cm⁻³ and its specific heat as 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, calculate the heat released per mole of water formed, in kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: $q = mc\Delta T = 150 \times 4.18 \times 6.7 = 4201$ J $= 4.201$ kJ; moles of water $= 0.075 \times 1.0 = 0.075$. Heat per mole $= 4.201/0.075 = 56.0$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The heat of neutralisation has the same value, about −57.1 kJ per mole of water, for every acid reacting with every base.
questions.solution_md: False. The value is constant only for a strong acid with a strong base; for a weak acid or weak base part of the energy is used up in ionisation, so less heat is released.

questions.stem_md: For a strong acid with a strong base in dilute solution, the heat of neutralisation is about ___ kJ per mole of water formed (magnitude).
questions.solution_md: The net reaction H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O releases about 57.1 kJ per mole of water.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The heat released when ethanoic acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide is less than 57.1 kJ per mole of water.

**Reason (R):** Ethanoic acid is completely ionised in dilute aqueous solution.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: about 55.2 kJ mol⁻¹ is released. R is false: ethanoic acid is only slightly ionised, and the energy needed to ionise the remaining acid (about 1.9 kJ mol⁻¹) reduces the heat released — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The heats of neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide and of nitric acid by potassium hydroxide are almost equal.

**Reason (R):** In each case the net change is the combination of one mole of H⁺(aq) with one mole of OH⁻(aq) to form water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. The other ions are spectators in both reactions, so the heat depends only on H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Write the ionic equation that is common to the neutralisation of every strong acid by every strong base in dilute solution, and state the enthalpy change per mole of water formed.

answer.model_answer_md: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹. A strong acid and a strong base are completely ionised, so the other ions are spectators and the heat of neutralisation is the same for all such pairs.

questions.solution_md: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O(l); −57.1 kJ per mole of water.

marking_scheme.step: ΔH = −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹ with the reason (complete ionisation)

questions.stem_md: The heat of neutralisation of ethanoic acid by sodium hydroxide is −55.2 kJ mol⁻¹, against −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹ for a strong acid and a strong base. Explain the difference and calculate the enthalpy of ionisation of ethanoic acid.

answer.model_answer_md: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid and is only partly ionised. As it is neutralised, more molecules must ionise, and this absorbs energy, so less heat is given out. Enthalpy of ionisation ≈ 57.1 − 55.2 = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: Weak acid must ionise, which absorbs energy

questions.stem_md: In a coffee-cup calorimeter, 100 cm³ of 0.50 M hydrochloric acid at 298.0 K is mixed with 100 cm³ of 0.50 M sodium hydroxide at the same temperature, and the highest temperature reached is 301.4 K. Taking the density of the mixture as 1 g cm⁻³ and its specific heat as 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, calculate the heat of neutralisation per mole of water and compare it with the accepted value of −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹.

answer.model_answer_md: $\Delta T = 301.4 - 298.0 = 3.4$ K; mass $= 200$ g. $q = mc\Delta T = 200 \times 4.18 \times 3.4 = 2842$ J. Moles of water $= 0.100 \times 0.50 = 0.050$. $\Delta H = -2.842/0.050 = -56.8$ kJ mol⁻¹, slightly less in magnitude than −57.1 because a little heat is lost to the surroundings.

questions.solution_md: $q = 2842$ J; $\Delta H \approx -56.8$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: The heats of neutralisation with sodium hydroxide are: hydrochloric acid −57.1, ethanoic acid −55.2 and hydrogen cyanide −12.1 kJ mol⁻¹. Arrange the three acids in order of increasing strength, and explain the trend by estimating the energy spent in ionising each weak acid.

answer.model_answer_md: The less heat is released, the weaker the acid, because more energy is needed to ionise it. Order of increasing strength: HCN < CH₃COOH < HCl. Energy spent on ionisation (relative to 57.1): ethanoic acid 57.1 − 55.2 = 1.9 kJ mol⁻¹; HCN 57.1 − 12.1 = 45.0 kJ mol⁻¹; HCl about zero, since it is already completely ionised.

questions.solution_md: HCN < CH₃COOH < HCl; ionisation 1.9 and 45.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain, with the ionic equation, why the heat of neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base is nearly constant. [2]

(b) A student mixes 40 cm³ of 1.0 M sulfuric acid with 60 cm³ of 1.0 M potassium hydroxide in an insulated cup. Taking the heat of neutralisation as −57.1 kJ per mole of water, a density of 1 g cm⁻³ and a specific heat of 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, calculate the rise in temperature. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A strong acid and a strong base are completely ionised in dilute solution, so the net reaction is always $\ce{H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l)}$ and the other ions are spectators; the heat released per mole of water is therefore the same, about 57.1 kJ.

(b) H⁺ $= 2 \times 0.040 = 0.080$ mol; OH⁻ $= 0.060$ mol, so the base is limiting and 0.060 mol of water forms. $q = 0.060 \times 57\,100 = 3426$ J. $\Delta T = q/(mc) = 3426/(100 \times 4.18) = 8.2$ K.

questions.solution_md: 0.060 mol of water; $\Delta T = 8.2$ K.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Complete ionisation; net equation H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
(a) Spectator ions, so same heat per mole

questions.stem_md: A student is told that the bond dissociation enthalpy of Cl–Cl is 242 kJ mol⁻¹. The standard enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine, $\ce{1/2Cl2(g) -> Cl(g)}$, is therefore:
questions.solution_md: Atomisation is defined per mole of gaseous atoms formed. Splitting one mole of Cl₂ gives two moles of Cl atoms for 242 kJ, so one mole of Cl atoms needs 242 / 2 = +121 kJ (endothermic, since bonds break) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which equation represents the enthalpy of sublimation of iodine?
questions.solution_md: Sublimation is the direct change from solid to vapour. I₂(g) → 2I(g) is bond dissociation, I₂(l) → I₂(g) is vaporisation, and I₂(s) → 2I(g) combines sublimation with dissociation — option (b).

questions.stem_md: For sodium, the enthalpy of sublimation is 107.3 kJ mol⁻¹ and the first ionisation enthalpy is 496 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy change for Na(s) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ is:
questions.solution_md: Na(s) → Na(g) takes 107.3 kJ; Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ takes 496 kJ. Total = 107.3 + 496 = 603.3 kJ mol⁻¹ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A polymer plant partly hydrogenates ethyne to ethene, $\ce{HC#CH(g) + H2(g) -> H2C=CH2(g)}$. Using C≡C 837, C=C 611, C–H 414 and H–H 436 kJ mol⁻¹, the estimated enthalpy change is:
questions.solution_md: Bonds broken: C≡C (837) + H–H (436) = 1273 kJ. Bonds formed: C=C (611) + 2 C–H (2 × 414) = 1439 kJ. ΔH = broken − formed = 1273 − 1439 = −166 kJ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The hydrogenation of ethyne to ethene is estimated at −166 kJ from bond enthalpies, but it comes to −174.4 kJ from enthalpies of formation. The main reason for the small difference is that:

options.text_md: bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds, not exact values for these molecules
enthalpies of formation are path functions and so vary with the route
bond enthalpies refer to the liquid state, but the reaction is in the gas phase
the reaction is not exothermic when calculated from bond enthalpies

questions.solution_md: From formation data ΔH = ΔfH(C₂H₄) − ΔfH(C₂H₂) = 52.3 − (226.7) = −174.4 kJ, a state-function calculation. A mean bond enthalpy (for example C–H 414) is the average over many different compounds, so a sum of such values is only an estimate — option (a).

questions.stem_md: On a cold, dry morning in Shimla, the frost on a parked car’s windscreen turns straight into water vapour in the sunshine without first melting. The enthalpy change for this change of state is the enthalpy of:

options.text_md: sublimation, and its sign is positive
fusion, and its sign is negative
vaporisation, and its sign is negative
deposition, and its sign is positive

questions.solution_md: Solid changing directly to vapour is sublimation. Molecules must be separated against their attractions, so heat is absorbed and ΔsubH is positive — option (a). Deposition is the reverse change and is exothermic.

questions.stem_md: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms of an element is formed from the element in its standard state, for example Na(s) → Na(g) or ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g), is called the enthalpy of ___.
questions.solution_md: This is the enthalpy of atomisation, ΔaH°; it is always positive. For a metal such as sodium it equals the enthalpy of sublimation.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The first ionisation enthalpy of a metal used to colour fireworks is the energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of its isolated gaseous atoms, and it is always positive.
questions.solution_md: True. Removing an electron from a gaseous atom, M(g) → M⁺(g) + e⁻, always needs energy, so ionisation enthalpy is positive.

questions.stem_md: Magnesium metal is vaporised in a flame and then ionised. Using ΔsubH(Mg) = 147.7, first ionisation enthalpy 738 and second ionisation enthalpy 1451 kJ mol⁻¹, calculate the enthalpy change for Mg(s) → Mg²⁺(g) + 2e⁻, in kJ mol⁻¹.

A steam-iron technician heats 36 g of ice at 0 °C until it is all steam at 100 °C. Use ΔfusH = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔvapH = 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ and a molar heat capacity of liquid water of 75.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (M of water = 18 g mol⁻¹). Calculate the heat absorbed in kJ.
questions.solution_md: Moles $= 36/18 = 2$. Per mole: melt $6.01$; warm $75.3 \times 100 / 1000 = 7.53$; boil $40.7$; total $= 54.24$ kJ. For 2 mol: $2 \times 54.24 = 108.48 \approx 108.5$ kJ.

questions.stem_md: The enthalpy change when one mole of a solid changes directly into its vapour, without passing through the liquid state, is the enthalpy of ___.
questions.solution_md: A direct solid-to-gas change is sublimation; for example I₂(s) → I₂(g).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Breaking a bond in a gaseous molecule is an endothermic process, and the same energy is released when the bond is formed.
questions.solution_md: True. Energy must be supplied to pull the bonded atoms apart (bond dissociation enthalpy, positive) and the same amount is released when they combine.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Bond formation is an endothermic process.

**Reason (R):** Energy must be supplied to bring two atoms together into a bond.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is false: forming a bond releases energy, so it is exothermic. R is false: energy is released, not supplied, when atoms combine; energy is needed to break the bond — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Match each enthalpy change with its equation.

options.text_md: Standard enthalpy of formation of ethyne
Standard enthalpy of combustion of ethanol

questions.solution_md: Formation of ethyne: elements → compound (r). Combustion of ethanol: the compound burnt in oxygen (p). Fusion: solid → liquid (s). First ionisation of Mg: Mg(g) → Mg⁺(g) + e⁻ (q).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the enthalpy of sublimation and the enthalpy of atomisation of iodine. Using ΔsubH(I₂) = 62.4 kJ mol⁻¹ and the I–I bond dissociation enthalpy of 151 kJ mol⁻¹ (both given), find the enthalpy change for I₂(s) → 2I(g).

answer.model_answer_md: Sublimation: I₂(s) → I₂(g), the solid changes directly to vapour. Atomisation: the element in its standard state is converted into gaseous atoms; for iodine, ½I₂(s) → I(g), per mole of atoms. For I₂(s) → 2I(g): 62.4 + 151 = 213.4 kJ mol⁻¹ (so 106.7 kJ per mole of I atoms).

questions.solution_md: 213.4 kJ mol⁻¹ for I₂(s) → 2I(g).

marking_scheme.step: Sublimation (solid → vapour) and atomisation (→ gaseous atoms) distinguished

questions.stem_md: A refrigeration engineer must melt 90 g of ice at 0 °C. Using the enthalpy of fusion of ice, 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ (M of water = 18 g mol⁻¹), calculate the heat absorbed, and say what happens to the temperature while the ice melts.

answer.model_answer_md: Moles of ice = 90 / 18 = 5 mol. Heat absorbed = 5 × 6.01 = 30.05 kJ. The temperature stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted, because the heat supplied goes into overcoming the forces holding the molecules in the solid, not into raising the temperature.

questions.solution_md: 30.05 kJ; temperature constant at 0 °C.

marking_scheme.step: Temperature constant during melting, with a reason

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why an enthalpy of reaction found from bond enthalpies is only an estimate, whereas one found from enthalpies of formation is accurate.

answer.model_answer_md: Bond enthalpies are mean values averaged over many compounds, so the C–H bond (for example) is not exactly 414 kJ mol⁻¹ in every molecule; and the method assumes all reactants and products are gases, so any change of state is ignored. Enthalpies of formation are measured values for the actual substances in their states.

questions.solution_md: Mean values; gas phase assumed.

marking_scheme.step: Gaseous state assumed; no change of state allowed for

questions.stem_md: A chemist chlorinates ethene in the gas phase, $\ce{C2H4(g) + Cl2(g) -> C2H4Cl2(g)}$, where C₂H₄Cl₂ is 1,2-dichloroethane, Cl–CH₂–CH₂–Cl. Using C=C 611, Cl–Cl 242, C–C 347 and C–Cl 326 kJ mol⁻¹, estimate the enthalpy change and say whether the reaction is exothermic.

answer.model_answer_md: Bonds broken: C=C (611) + Cl–Cl (242) = 853 kJ. Bonds formed: C–C (347) + 2 C–Cl (2 × 326 = 652) = 999 kJ. ΔH = 853 − 999 = −146 kJ mol⁻¹; negative, so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.solution_md: ΔH = −146 kJ mol⁻¹, exothermic.

questions.stem_md: A student estimates the enthalpy of atomisation of propane, C₃H₈(g) → 3C(g) + 8H(g), in two ways. (i) From bond enthalpies C–H 414 and C–C 347 kJ mol⁻¹; (ii) from ΔfH(C₃H₈) = −103.8, ΔsubH(C) = 716.7 and the H–H bond enthalpy 436 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate both and comment.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Propane has 8 C–H and 2 C–C bonds: 8 × 414 + 2 × 347 = 4006 kJ mol⁻¹. (ii) Elements → atoms: 3 × 716.7 + 4 × 436 = 3894.1 kJ; the compound lies 103.8 kJ below the elements, so ΔatomH = 3894.1 − (-103.8) = 3125.9 kJ mol⁻¹. The two values agree to within 0.3 %, since mean bond enthalpies are averages.

questions.solution_md: (i) 4006; (ii) 3125.9 kJ mol⁻¹; close agreement.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define bond dissociation enthalpy and enthalpy of atomisation, with one equation for each. [2]

(b) Calculate the enthalpy of atomisation of ethyne, C₂H₂(g) → 2C(g) + 2H(g), from ΔfH(C₂H₂) = +226.7 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔsubH(C) = 716.7 kJ mol⁻¹ and the H–H bond enthalpy 436 kJ mol⁻¹, and compare it with the value 2 × 414 + 837 from mean bond enthalpies. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The bond dissociation enthalpy is the enthalpy change when one mole of a particular bond in a gaseous molecule is broken, e.g. $\ce{H2(g) -> 2H(g)}$, +436 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy of atomisation is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element (or compound), e.g. $\ce{C(graphite) -> C(g)}$, +716.7 kJ mol⁻¹.

(b) Elements → atoms: $2 \times 716.7 + 436 = 1869.4$ kJ. Ethyne lies 226.7 kJ above the elements, so $\Delta_{atom}H = 1869.4 - 226.7 = 1642.7$ kJ mol⁻¹. The bond-enthalpy estimate is $2 \times 414 + 837 = 1665$ kJ mol⁻¹, within about 1.4 % of it, because mean bond enthalpies are averages.

questions.solution_md: (b) $\Delta_{atom}H = 1642.7$ kJ mol⁻¹ against 1665 from bond enthalpies.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Estimate the enthalpy of combustion of ethyne gas, C₂H₂(g) + 5/2 O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + H₂O(g), from the mean bond enthalpies C–H 414, C≡C 837, O=O 498, C=O 799 and O–H 463 kJ mol⁻¹. [3]

(b) The value from enthalpies of formation (CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(g) −241.8, C₂H₂ +226.7 kJ mol⁻¹) is also needed: calculate it and suggest a reason for the difference. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Bonds broken: 2 C–H (828) + C≡C (837) + 5/2 O=O (1245) = 2910 kJ. Bonds formed: 4 C=O (3196) + 2 O–H (926) = 4122 kJ. ΔH = 2910 − 4122 = −1212 kJ mol⁻¹.

(b) ΔH = [2(−393.5) + (−241.8)] − (+226.7) = −1255.5 kJ mol⁻¹. The bond-enthalpy estimate is about 44 kJ less negative because it uses mean bond enthalpies (for example, the C=O bond in CO₂ is not exactly 799 kJ mol⁻¹).

questions.solution_md: (a) −1212 kJ mol⁻¹; (b) −1255.5 kJ mol⁻¹; mean bond enthalpies.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Bonds formed 4122 kJ and ΔH = −1212 kJ mol⁻¹
(b) Mean bond enthalpies as the reason

questions.stem_md: Which statement is Hess’s law of constant heat summation?

options.text_md: the enthalpy change of a reaction depends on the number of steps in which it takes place
the heat of a reaction is independent of the temperature
the total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it takes place in one step or in several steps
the enthalpy change of a reaction doubles when the number of moles of products doubles but not of the reactants

questions.solution_md: Hess’s law states that the overall enthalpy change depends only on the initial and final states, not on the route or the number of steps — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Hess’s law is a direct consequence of the fact that enthalpy is:

options.text_md: a path function, depending on how the change is carried out
a state function, depending only on the initial and final states
an extensive property only, with no other special feature

questions.solution_md: Because H is a state function, ΔH for a change depends only on the initial and final states, so the same ΔH results by any route — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a jewellery research lab the enthalpies of combustion are measured as −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ for graphite and −395.4 kJ mol⁻¹ for diamond. The enthalpy change for C(graphite) → C(diamond) is:
questions.solution_md: Graphite → CO₂ (−393.5) followed by CO₂ → diamond (reverse of −395.4, so +395.4). Sum = −393.5 + 395.4 = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The enthalpy of combustion of methane is −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹. For the reverse process in a laboratory model, $\ce{2CO2(g) + 4H2O(l) -> 2CH4(g) + 4O2(g)}$, the enthalpy change is:
questions.solution_md: Reversing a reaction changes the sign of ΔH, and doubling the amounts doubles it: ΔH = −2 × (−890.3) = +1780.6 kJ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The enthalpy of solution of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is −66.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of the pentahydrate is +11.7 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy change for $\ce{CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l) -> CuSO4.5H2O(s)}$ is:
questions.solution_md: Dissolve the anhydrous salt (−66.5), then reverse the dissolution of the hydrate (−11.7): ΔH = −66.5 − 11.7 = −78.2 kJ mol⁻¹ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the first step of nitric acid manufacture, $\ce{4NH3(g) + 5O2(g) -> 4NO(g) + 6H2O(g)}$. Using ΔfH (NH₃ −46.1, NO +90.3, H₂O(g) −241.8 kJ mol⁻¹), the enthalpy change is:
For a smog-chamber study, N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g) has ΔH = +180.6 kJ and 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) has ΔH = −114.2 kJ (both given). Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of NO₂(g) in kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Adding the equations: $\ce{N2(g) + 2O2(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$, $\Delta H = 180.6 + (-114.2) = 66.4$ kJ for 2 mol. Per mole of NO₂: $66.4/2 = 33.2$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The enthalpy change for converting reactants into products is the same by every route, provided the initial and final states are the same.
questions.solution_md: True. This is Hess’s law, which holds because enthalpy is a state function.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The enthalpy change for converting graphite to carbon dioxide is the same whether the carbon is burnt directly or first converted to carbon monoxide.

**Reason (R):** The heat released in a chemical change depends on the path followed between the initial and final states.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true by Hess’s law: −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ either way (−110.5 plus −283.0). R is false: enthalpy is a state function, so the total heat does not depend on the path — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A bio-fuel chemist wants the enthalpy change for the hydration of ethene, $\ce{C2H4(g) + H2O(l) -> C2H5OH(l)}$. Use Hess's law with ΔfH values (C₂H₄ +52.3, H₂O(l) −285.8, C₂H₅OH(l) −277.7 kJ mol⁻¹) to calculate it.

answer.model_answer_md: Route: reactants → elements → product. $\Delta H = \Delta_fH(\text{product}) - \Delta_fH(\text{reactants}) = -277.7 - (+52.3 - 285.8) = -277.7 + 233.5 = -44.2$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: $\Delta H = -44.2$ kJ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: Σ products − Σ reactants set up

questions.stem_md: Ethyne cannot be made directly from its elements in a calorimeter. Use Hess's law to find the enthalpy of formation of ethyne from the enthalpies of combustion: C(graphite) −393.5, H₂(g) −285.8 and C₂H₂(g) −1299.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

answer.model_answer_md: Target: $\ce{2C(graphite) + H2(g) -> C2H2(g)}$. Add: $2 \times$ (C + O₂ → CO₂) $= 2(-393.5)$; (H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O) $= -285.8$; reverse of ethyne combustion $= +1299.5$. $\Delta_fH = -787.0 - 285.8 + 1299.5 = +226.7$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: $\Delta_fH = +226.7$ kJ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: Target equation and choice of equations
Reverse the ethyne combustion; multiply C by 2

questions.stem_md: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns blue as it takes up water. Using the enthalpy of solution of $\ce{CuSO4(s)}$, −66.5 kJ mol⁻¹, and of $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O(s)}$, +11.7 kJ mol⁻¹, draw an enthalpy cycle and calculate the enthalpy of hydration for $\ce{CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l) -> CuSO4.5H2O(s)}$.

answer.model_answer_md: Cycle: anhydrous salt + 5H₂O → hydrate (ΔH_hyd, unknown) and both → the same aqueous solution of CuSO₄. By Hess's law $\Delta H_{hyd} + (+11.7) = -66.5$, so $\Delta H_{hyd} = -66.5 - 11.7 = -78.2$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: $\Delta H_{hyd} = -78.2$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: In a hydrogen plant, methane reacts with steam: $\ce{CH4(g) + H2O(g) -> CO(g) + 3H2(g)}$. Calculate the enthalpy change from ΔfH (CH₄ −74.8, H₂O(g) −241.8, CO −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹), say whether the reaction is endothermic or exothermic, and state the effect on the heat needed of making twice as much hydrogen.

answer.model_answer_md: $\Delta H = [-110.5 + 3(0)] - [-74.8 + (-241.8)] = -110.5 + 316.6 = +206.1$ kJ mol⁻¹, endothermic. For twice the quantity of reaction, ΔH is doubled: $+412.2$ kJ, so the heat required doubles.

questions.solution_md: $\Delta H = +206.1$ kJ mol⁻¹, endothermic; heat doubles.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State Hess's law and explain why it holds. [2]

(b) Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of liquid ethanol from the enthalpies of combustion of graphite (−393.5), hydrogen (−285.8) and liquid ethanol (−1366.7 kJ mol⁻¹). Write the target equation and the cycle you use. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or in several steps, provided the initial and final states are the same. It holds because enthalpy is a state function.

(b) Target: $\ce{2C(graphite) + 3H2(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> C2H5OH(l)}$. Combine: $2 \times$ (C + O₂ → CO₂) $= 2(-393.5)$; $3 \times$ (H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l)) $= 3(-285.8)$; reverse of ethanol combustion $= +1366.7$. $\Delta_fH = -787.0 - 857.4 + 1366.7 = -277.7$ kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: $\Delta_fH = -277.7$ kJ mol⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Correct use of 2, 3 and the reversed combustion

questions.stem_md:
(a) Why is the enthalpy of combustion of carbon (graphite) the same number as the enthalpy of formation of carbon dioxide? [2]

(b) Calculate the enthalpy of combustion of carbon monoxide, $\ce{CO(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> CO2(g)}$, from ΔfH (CO −110.5, CO₂ −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹), and the calorific value of carbon monoxide (M = 28 g mol⁻¹) in kJ g⁻¹. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Burning graphite gives $\ce{C(graphite) + O2(g) -> CO2(g)}$. This is also the reaction that forms one mole of CO₂ from its elements in their standard states (graphite is the standard state of carbon), so the same equation and enthalpy serve for both definitions.

(b) $\Delta_cH = -393.5 - (-110.5) = -283.0$ kJ mol⁻¹. Calorific value $= 283.0/28 = 10.1$ kJ g⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: $\Delta_cH = -283.0$ kJ mol⁻¹; 10.1 kJ g⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Graphite is the standard state of carbon

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define the calorific value of a fuel and state its unit. [2]

(b) Hydrogen (ΔcH = −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹, M = 2) is proposed as a bus fuel in place of ethanol (ΔcH = −1366.7 kJ mol⁻¹, M = 46). Calculate the calorific value of each, and the mass of ethanol that gives the same heat as 1.00 kg of hydrogen. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The calorific value is the heat produced when unit mass of a fuel is burnt completely; its unit is kJ g⁻¹ (or kJ kg⁻¹).

(b) Hydrogen: $285.8/2 = 142.9$ kJ g⁻¹. Ethanol: $1366.7/46 = 29.7$ kJ g⁻¹. Heat from 1.00 kg H₂ $= 1000 \times 142.9 = 142900$ kJ; mass of ethanol $= 142900/29.71 = 4810$ g $\approx 4.81$ kg.

questions.solution_md: 142.9 and 29.7 kJ g⁻¹; about 4.81 kg of ethanol.
